results.title: Secret funds, public money, public accountability
results.description: Confidential and intelligence funds (CIFs) exist for a legitimate purpose: protecting the state when secrecy is essential to protecting lives, operations and national security. But secrecy should never be synonymous to weak accountability. The controversy surrounding the alleged misuse of confidential and intelligence funds has been there for a while—an institutional problem in which public money can be difficult for the public, and sometimes even auditors, to trace. It is once again in the limelight in the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. This is precisely why the 2027 national budget presents an opportunity for Congress to fix what went wrong in the past. The proposed ₱7.2-trillion 2027 national budget is now before Congress, with transparency and efficient spending identified by the government as priorities. Congress should translate those promises into concrete safeguards for CIFs, rather than merely adjust their amounts. The first reform should be categorical: confidential funds should be restricted to agencies with a clear national-security, law-enforcement or intelligence mandate. Civilian offices whose primary functions are education, social welfare, health, administration or public information should not routinely receive CIFs simply because an executive official asserts a need for surveillance. Existing budget rules already recognize that confidential expenses concern surveillance activities in civilian agencies, while intelligence expenses involve information-gathering with a direct impact on national security. The better question is whether civilian agencies need such extraordinary funds at all. If exceptional circumstances justify an allocation, Congress should require a written justification, measurable objectives, a defined spending ceiling and periodic review. No CIF should be treated as a discretionary political fund. Second, COA oversight must be strengthened, not diluted by confidentiality. Existing Joint Circular No. 2015-01 already provides rules for the entitlement, release, use, reporting and audit of CIFs. But rules are meaningful only when documentation, verification and consequences are real. Every peso should have a secure audit trail—from authorization and withdrawal to recipient, purpose, accomplishment and liquidation—while protecting genuinely sensitive operational information. Third, accountability must attach to people, not merely offices. The official who requests, approves, receives, disburses or certifies CIF expenditures must be identifiable and answerable. Quarterly accomplishment reports should go beyond saying money was “utilized.” They should explain what objective was pursued, what activities were undertaken, what measurable results were achieved and why the expenditure was necessary. Existing budget provisions already require quarterly reporting on CIF accomplishments. Congress should make those reports substantive and enforce penalties for false, incomplete or deliberately misleading certifications. There must also be consequences. Unsupported, unauthorized or demonstrably improper expenditures should trigger disallowance, restitution and administrative or criminal proceedings where warranted. Public office cannot be a shield against personal responsibility. Finally, accountability cannot rest on COA and Congress alone. Filipinos can examine budget documents, attend legislative hearings, support credible investigative journalism, report irregularities through lawful channels and demand answers from elected representatives. Citizens need not know operational secrets; they have every right to know whether public money produced legitimate public results. National security deserves resources. But national security also deserves public trust. The 2027 budget should therefore make one principle unmistakable: confidentiality may protect an operation, but it must never protect misuse. Confidential and intelligence funds should be necessary, narrowly defined, traceable, auditable and personally accountable. Anything less risks turning a tool designed to protect the Republic into a loophole that undermines it.

results.title: Hidden economic opportunities in raising native poultry and livestock
results.description: AVANT GARDENER We tend not to think too much about our native breeds, often them to backyard livestock, not a viable long-term source of income. Dr. Rene Santiago, Agricultural Center Chief of the Department of Science and Technology’s. National Swine and Poultry Research and Development Center, wants to dissuade us of this mindset. Established in 1995, the NSPRDC initially involved “all commodities with regards to swine and poultry.” The Center shifted its focus to native animals in 2010 with the establishment of the Philippine Native Animal Development Program. “It's a Department of Agriculture program looking for the potential [in native animals],” Santiago said. Before this, a “native chicken” was just a native chicken. There were no distinct breeds or strains. “Now we have the Darag, Banaba, the Parawakan,” Santiago said. “There are different characteristics and they are now propagated through the type, and they now have standards comparable to the commercial hybrid developed in the West.” It’s the same for native pigs. “We have the Kalinga, Quezon black, Marinduque, Isabela, Samar, and I think Benguet is introducing their own breeds now.” The Center also developed and introduced the popular Itik Pinas via the Development of Sustainable Breeder Mallard Duck Production System, a DOST PCARRD funded the project, helmed by Santiago that aimed to develop a signature Philippine duck breed. “It was the start of the avian influenza spread in Asia, and we didn’t have enough ducks, so we looked to conserve, to improve, and propagate quality itik or duck for the purpose of balut and salted egg, our local delicacies,” he said. Through the Center’s interventions, the itik went from laying an average of 200-210 eggs to 253 eggs annually. The breed is now used in government breder farms and is part of a national distribution collaboration with the private sector. Why develop native breeds? This was the question asked when the program started. After all, weren’t these farm animals already ubiquitous? And weren’t they smaller than Western hybrids? Santiago lists three main reasons. Resiliency. Native animals can thrive on food sources commonly found around small farms, and even households. “We have breeds now, and they may not be fast growers, but they have [specific] qualities that we found while characterizing those native species,” Santiago said. “ Even native cattle have an advantage. Santiago cited the native cattle from Panay, who, because of their small stature, can be raised healthy in a small tract of land. “Our ducks don't [need] vaccination. We only vaccinate our native chickens one to two times. [Hybrid] layers need 18 vaccinations before they can lay eggs,” Santiago said. “If you’re adapted to local conditions, you tend to have higher immunity.” Product demand. Native breeds may be smaller than foreign hybrids, but they do taste better in Filipino dishes. “One is balut,” Santiago said. “Our ducks have bigger eggs, more than 65 grams to 70 grams compared to other ducks in Taiwan and China because we prefer big balut. The eggs also have thick shells and the ducks can also be raised in rice fields.” Most people prefer native chicken for tinola and other traditional chicken soups. “Darag is very popular in the Visayas. it's small, but good for binakol,” Santiago said. Native pigs are preferred for lechon. “One basic characteristic is the crispiness. It lasts longer. I think it's correlated to the longer period of maturation,” Santiago said. “Commercial pigs grow faster, so they are younger, so their skin is not good for lechon.” Opportunity for export . If a product is developed well, there’s always the possibility of finding markets overseas. Santiago uses the Itik Pinas as an example. “There’s an export opportunity for salted eggs because we have an overproduction of ducks,” he said. “In order to promote native animals, we should take the opportunity to export their products.” Though much progress has been made, there is still a long way to go. “We need to develop and utilize our local feed resources... Those sophisticated feeding ingredients are not suited for native animals. They have their own requirements,” Santiago said, adding that commercial feeds are also too expensive for many small farmers. “In UP Los Baños, they said our native pigs have a good utilization for fibrous feed ingredients [like] grasses, legumes, and root crops... which is why they have difficulty digesting commercial feed, [whose ingredients, like soy and coconut], are selected for easy pelleting.” Interested parties can contact the Center through social media. They are targetting the release of 28,000 ducks this year through DA Regional Field Offices, almost three times the previous requirement. The Center also offers books on native livestock, including one that documents the experiences and best practices of native livestock raisers around the country. Santiago said the Center’s goal is simple: “Produce food in general for small farmers.” And if we reframe the way we look at native livestock and poultry, we’ll see that they can offer a good way for this goal to be achieved.

results.title: They have renounced marriage
results.description: REFLECTIONS TODAY Because of Jesus’ prohibition of divorce, his disciples say that it is better not to marry. Jesus says that some people (“born so”) are “incapable of marriage” (v 12). A eunuch (Greek eunouxoi) refers to a man or a boy deprived of functioning male organs (v 12). He may also be a castrated man (“made so by others”) placed in charge of a harem or employed as a chamberlain in a palace (v 12). But there are also “eunuchs”—persons who are otherwise physically normal, but who renounce marriage for the sake of the Kingdom of heaven. These are persons who take on celibacy as a personal choice or upon entering priesthood in the Catholic Church. Then there are consecrated men [and women] who take the evangelical vow of chastity, along with the vows of poverty and obedience. In a culture where the Mosaic Law calls on the Israelites to “be fertile, then, and multiply” (Gn 9:7), Jesus remained celibate as a sign of total self-giving to the cause of the Kingdom of heaven. And he invites those who can accept this [renouncing marriage] to accept it. In turn, Paul advices the unmarried woman, if she has the gift of “vocation,” to remain unmarried so as to wholly concern herself about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in both body and spirit (1 Cor 7:34). Paul himself was probably not married (cf 1 Cor 9:5). Both marriage and celibacy are paths to holiness. Marriage is a sacrament that mirrors Christ’s relationship with the Church, characterized by love, fidelity, and self-giving. Celibacy, on the other hand, is a radical commitment to God, a sign of the Kingdom to come, where we are fully united with the Lord. Whether in marriage, celibacy, or other forms of dedication to God—each path is a unique gift from God and a means for growing closer to him. Source: “365 Days with the Lord 2026,” St. Paul’s, 7708 St. Paul Rd., SAV, Makati City (Phils.); Tel.: 632-895-9701; E-mail: publishing@stpauls.ph; Website: http://www.stpauls.ph.

results.title: Beyond supporting local
results.description: EDITORS DESK In the cause of moving Philippine fashion and design forward, I have always been an enthusiastic supporter of homegrown, locally produced products. When there is a new collection from a Filipino label, I’m there at the launch to see it. When a local designer launches a new collection, I am often among those willing to put my money where my advocacy is. I believe in Filipino talent. I believe that our designers, craftsmen, makers, and creatives can create work that deserves to be seen not only here but around the world. Supporting local is, for me, more than a slogan. It is something I genuinely believe in and try to practice. But supporting local also means being honest when something falls short. Recently, I had two experiences with local brands that made me think about the other side of the “support local” conversation: If we expect consumers to champion Filipino brands, shouldn’t brands also step up and give consumers a reason to keep coming back? The first instance involved a clothing label that has been featured in numerous magazines and has made an impressive appearance at a fashion week. I enthusiastically ordered a complete look straight from the runway. I contacted the designer online, paid in full, and was told that I would be updated when the order was ready. That updated never came. Three months passed. With no message, I finally reached out to ask about the order. A few days later, the designer apologized and told me that the order had never been put in. For three months, I had essentially been waiting for something that wasn’t even in production. The designer offered another look from the collection that was already available. I almost accepted. But it wasn’t exactly what I wanted, and after three months of waiting, I was already questioning the business process. I eventually requested a full refund. It was granted but the refund itself took another three weeks. Another experience happened just last month. I discovered a proudly Marikina-made shoe brand through social media, and was drawn to its story of building a local footwear business today. I visited its showroom and placed a custom order with the brand’s interns, as they were the only people there present to take my order. To be sure, I repeated the order through Instagram with the owner. I paid in full and was told it would take two to three weeks. Six weeks later, the shoes arrived. In the wrong size. What made it more frustrating was the lack of communication throughout the process. There were no updates or messages unless I initiated them. The brand had to restart production, and eventually the second pair arrived correctly, made to my specifications. I got what I wanted in the end. But getting there was an ordeal. These experiences are not meant to discourage anyone from buying local. Quite the opposite, actually. They are reminders of why local brands need to take their businesses as seriously as consumers take their support. The products I ordered were not inexpensive. And while I am willing to pay a premium for good design, craftsmanship, and the opportunity to support a young budding Filipino business, that expectation extends beyond the product itself. The customer experience is part of the product. A beautifully designed outfit does not excuse poor communication. A well-crafted shoe does not excuse a wrong size. Being a small or emerging brand may explain why systems are still being developed, but it cannot become a permanent excuse for lapses in service. I also understand the challenges. Many local labels operate with small teams, limited resources, and production systems that are nowhere near the scale of more established brands. But perhaps this is precisely why better systems matter. A simple order tracker, a confirmation message, a realistic production timeline, or a proactive update can make a tremendous difference. There is also a bigger conversation we need to have about the price of local fashion and design. I often hear from people in media, fashion, and consumers that some Filipino brands have become expensive enough to be accessible only to a particular segment of the market. If we want “buy local” to become more than an aspirational idea, affordability and value have to be part of the conversation, too. I will continue to support local. I will continue to celebrate Filipino creativity and champion designers who are pushing the industry forward. But support should not mean blind loyalty. If we truly want Philippine fashion and design to compete globally, our standards have to be global, too—not just in creativity and craftsmanship, but in professionalism, communication, service, and the entire customer experience. We ask consumers to believe in local. Local brands, in turn, have to give us every reason to believe. (Rey Robes Ilagan is the editor of Manila Bulletin’s Lifestyle section.)

results.title: Infrastructure sets the ceiling
results.description: NIGHT OWL We often tell women to dream bigger, work harder and claim their place in public life. Yet ambition does not grow in a vacuum. It depends on the systems around it: safe transport, affordable childcare, reliable healthcare, decent housing, accessible education, flexible workplaces and strong social protection. When these systems are weak, women do not simply face inconvenience. Their choices shrink. Infrastructure is usually discussed as roads, bridges and power grids. But for women, infrastructure also includes the care services that make paid work possible. A mother cannot pursue a promotion if the nearest day-care center is too expensive, too far away or closes before her shift ends. A young woman cannot accept a job across town if public transport is unsafe after dark. A woman with a disability cannot participate equally when workplaces, buses and public buildings remain inaccessible. This is why infrastructure sets the ceiling. Talent may determine how high someone could rise, but infrastructure determines whether she can enter the building at all. The burden is even heavier for women from marginalized backgrounds. Low-income women, migrants, racial and ethnic minorities, rural women, single mothers and women with disabilities often face several barriers at once. They are more likely to work in insecure jobs, live far from employment centers, rely on overstretched public services and carry unpaid caring responsibilities. When support is missing, privilege fills the gap. Families with money can buy childcare, private transport, tutoring and domestic help. Families without money must sacrifice time, income or opportunity. So we should ask a more honest question: how much support are we actually giving women to pursue their own careers? Too often, society celebrates women who “manage it all” while ignoring the exhaustion and invisible labor behind that achievement. We praise resilience when we should be building systems that make constant resilience unnecessary. A career should not depend on whether a woman has grandparents nearby, a partner with flexible hours or enough income to pay for private care. Day-care centers are a crucial test of our priorities. Affordable, high-quality childcare is not a private luxury; it is economic infrastructure. It allows parents, especially mothers, to remain in employment, study, build businesses and accept leadership roles. It also gives children safe environments in which to learn and develop. Yet in many communities, childcare remains scarce, costly or poorly matched to working hours. Shift workers, informal workers and rural families are particularly badly served. Without sustained investment, public promises of equality remain hollow, because opportunity is still rationed according to income, geography, family structure and the amount of unpaid care a woman can personally absorb. The same principle applies to elder care, reproductive healthcare, parental leave and workplace flexibility. Women are still expected to absorb the gaps in public provision. When a child is sick, a relative needs care or transport fails, it is usually women’s paid work that bends or breaks. Building inclusive infrastructure requires more than adding a few facilities. Services must be affordable, safe, accessible and designed around real lives. Governments should expand public childcare, support community-based centers, improve transport safety and ensure that social protection reaches informal workers. Employers should offer predictable schedules, paid family leave and genuine flexibility without penalizing career progression. Men must also be expected and enabled to share care equally. The question is not whether women are ambitious enough. The question is whether our institutions are prepared to support that ambition. Until care, mobility, safety and access are treated as foundations of equality, women will continue to be told the sky is the limit while standing beneath a ceiling built by inadequate infrastructure.
